A startup reports its Firebase bill jumped from $25 to $1750 per month after a billing change with no notice. The reporting tools gave no visibility into what was driving the increase. They say Firebase ignored their emails for over a month and offered no phone contact.

A user finds Firebase easy, useful and constantly improving (e.g., cloud functions), but calls its support a joke. Only 5 one-on-one email support questions are allowed per year, even for urgent requests while paying a lot and scaling. Firebase also doesn't respond on Twitter.

Another team also went from ~$25/mo to $1000–2000/mo with the pricing change. They had 3–4 downtime incidents of over an hour in two months, with no way to contact anyone except a web form. They are now shipping replacements for their Firebase usage.

Commenters were shocked that billed usage included failed attempts blocked by security rules. An explanation offered: not using keep-alive/TLS session resumption with the REST API inflated metered bandwidth. Firebase had previously been under-counting it, then started counting without warning.

An indie dev uses Firebase Database at arm's length. They avoid proprietary features and treat it only as a JSON store they can export to another NoSQL DBaaS. As a solo developer, they can't spend time maintaining a secure, high-availability database themselves.
A user got a $1k Firebase charge from someone running an automated script to hammer their endpoint just to drive up the price.

Firebase API keys are embedded in client code because Google described them as 'public by design.' Commenters note those same Google API keys could later authenticate to Gemini, leading to surprise bills. Firebase docs were quietly updated to say Firebase keys should be used only for Firebase APIs.
Users point out there is no way to hard-cap billing on GCP/Firebase, only notifications. Spending data isn't real-time, so even an automated shutoff can fire too late after thousands are spent.

A developer built a real-time whiteboarding app for teachers on the original Firebase service over 10 years ago. It was fast enough to run basic collision physics of letter tiles and sync their positions to multiple clients at once.

A user praises Firebase's separation of data retrieval/update logic from access-policy enforcement. You can prototype the happy path and add rules later, confident you aren't leaking data, since queries are checked before execution. However, developers often don't grasp how the mechanism works at first.
A developer whose app is built on Firebase says they are keenly aware of the cost of lock-in as traffic escalates.

One commenter says Firebase is notorious for an unintuitive lack of server-side query options once you start using it. Another says, besides pricing, the painful part is storage rules: they have to be reimplemented if you switch away.

A huge Firebase fan says what makes it special is the glue. Account management and libraries come free, and the tools work together seamlessly, so the 'boring' parts are handled and you can focus on the interesting parts.

A user calls Firebase invaluable and its free plan and limits very generous. They have APIs in production running solely on Firebase Functions with Firestore, and see auth, hosting, Functions and the CLI as huge features.
Firebase documentation is limited to its docs and YouTube channel, which can feel thin once you get past 'get-started' depth.
An early user (ID 68) says it took about 5 hours to add real-time notifications to one of their products with Firebase.
An Angular user built their business on AngularFire, calling it one of the most amazing things about Firebase. They say Firebase really cares about developer experience.
A user who had just started on Firebase decided to move off after the Google acquisition. They expected Google not to care about paying customers and feared either a shutdown or vendor lock-in.
A user complains Firebase lacks a count query: to count children they have to download all the data.
A team that has used Firebase for a while says it's one of the best systems they've used in a long time. They want a deeper querying language or a realtime export to Postgres for SQL-style analytics.
